warmup.q: Your team adds a field merchantId with no default to the Avro schema of the payments values. The subject has the registry's default compatibility mode. What happens when the new producer tries to register it?
options: It's accepted: adding a field never breaks old consumers
It's rejected with HTTP 409: consumers on the new schema couldn't read old records
It's accepted, and old records read merchantId as null
It's accepted, and the registry adds an empty default
warmup.why: The default mode is BACKWARD: a reader on the new schema must read data written with the latest one. Old records have no merchantId, and with no default the reader can't fill it, so the registry refuses the version (HTTP 409, error code 40901). The first option is true under FORWARD, where old readers skip the new field. Avro never invents a default or a null for a field that has none.

sections.h: A producer changes a field, and every consumer breaks
sections.html:
The payment service publishes each payment as JSON: {"id": "pay-1", "account": "acct-17", "amount": 4000}, the amount in cents. Six teams consume it. One morning the payment team renames amount to amountMinor, because a new currency has three decimal places, and deploys. The ledger consumer looks for amount, finds nothing, and posts 0.00. Nobody gets an exception.

Kafka can't stop this. A broker stores a value as bytes and never looks inside it (lesson 1). And the change can't be undone cleanly: records written in the new shape stay in the log for the whole retention period, and every replay reads both shapes.

The simplest fix is a shared document, or a shared jar with the Payment class, and a promise to change it carefully. It breaks on time. Producers and consumers deploy on different days, the log holds records written by last month's code, and a document can't refuse a bad change. So two things are needed: each record must say which version of the schema wrote it, and something must check a new version against the old ones before any producer uses it.

A schema is the written-down shape of a record: field names, types, defaults. With Avro, a common format for Kafka values, the schema is JSON and the data is compact binary with no field names in it. The Try-it encodes the payment above in 16 bytes, against 53 for the JSON above. The catch: you can't read Avro bytes without the writer's schema. Without it they are just three values in a row.

Schema Registry stores the schemas. It's a small HTTP service; each topic's values get a subject, payments-value by default, with numbered versions. The producer's serializer registers its schema (or looks it up), gets a numeric id, and writes 5 bytes before the Avro data: a magic byte 0 and the id in 4 bytes. The consumer's deserializer reads the id, fetches that schema once and caches it.

Now the consumer holds two schemas: the writer's, found by id, and its own reader's schema, compiled into its code. Avro resolves them field by field, by name. A field the writer has and the reader doesn't is skipped. A field the reader has and the writer doesn't gets the reader's default; with no default, the read fails. That one rule decides which changes are safe.

Java
// the consumer's side: the writer's schema comes by id, the reader's schema is the consumer's own
Schema writer = registry.schemaById(schemaIdFromTheFirst5Bytes);
var reader = new GenericDatumReader<GenericRecord>(writer, myPaymentSchema);
GenericRecord payment = reader.read(null, DecoderFactory.get().binaryDecoder(avroBytes, null));
Kotlin
// the consumer's side: the writer's schema comes by id, the reader's schema is the consumer's own
val writer: Schema = registry.schemaById(schemaIdFromTheFirst5Bytes)
val reader = GenericDatumReader<GenericRecord>(writer, myPaymentSchema)
val payment: GenericRecord = reader.read(null, DecoderFactory.get().binaryDecoder(avroBytes, null))

(registry.schemaById stands for what the registry-aware deserializer does for you.)

try.title: Read one payment with three reader schemas
steps: Run AvroEvolutionDemo from the labs folder (command below). No broker, no registry: Avro's own library on your JVM.
It writes a payment with schema v1, then reads the same bytes with v1, with v2 (adds currency with a default) and with v3 (adds merchantId with none). Predict which reads fail before it prints.

v1 payment as Avro binary, 16 bytes: 0a 70 61 79 2d 31 0e 61 63 63 74 2d 31 37 c0 3e
with the 5-byte registry prefix, 21 bytes: 00 00 00 00 01 | ...
reader v1 reads it: {"id": "pay-1", "account": "acct-17", "amount": 4000}
reader v2 reads it: {"id": "pay-1", "account": "acct-17", "amount": 4000, "currency": "EUR"}

The 16 bytes hold no field names: 0a is the length of "pay-1" (5, which Avro's zigzag encoding stores as 10, hex 0a), then its five bytes; 0e and "acct-17"; c0 3e is 4000 as a variable-length long. The registry prefix adds a 0 byte and the schema id. Reader v2 filled currency from its default; reader v3 had nothing to fill merchantId with. Avro's SchemaCompatibility gives the same verdicts as the reads.

sections.h: Compatibility modes decide which changes the registry accepts
sections.html:
Before it registers a new version, the registry checks it against the versions it already has, with the Avro rule above. The direction of the check is the subject's compatibility mode.

The default is BACKWARD: a consumer on the new schema must be able to read data written with the latest registered one. That protects replays, because the topic still holds old records. Adding a field with a default passes; adding one without a default fails, since old records don't have it. Under BACKWARD you upgrade consumers first, and once they read the new version, producers can start writing it.

FORWARD checks the other direction: a consumer still on the latest version must read data written with the new one. Adding a field always passes, because old readers skip it; removing a field passes only if old readers have a default for it. Producers upgrade first. FULL requires both, so only fields with defaults may come or go, in any deploy order. NONE checks nothing.

Each mode has a _TRANSITIVE twin that checks every registered version, not just the latest. That matters for compacted topics and long retention, where version 1 records live as long as the topic. Version 3 can read version 2 and still fail on version 1.

Change BACKWARD FORWARD FULL
Add a field with a default yes yes yes
Add a field without a default no yes no
Remove a field that had a default yes yes yes
Remove a field without a default yes no no
Widen int to long yes no no
Rename a field no no no

The format changes the details. Avro needs the writer's schema to read anything, and defaults drive its evolution, as above. Protobuf writes a field number before each value, so a reader skips unknown fields without the writer's schema; renaming a field costs nothing, and reusing a field number corrupts data. Confluent recommends BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE for Protobuf. JSON Schema keeps readable JSON on the wire, with bigger records, and whether a change is compatible depends on whether the schema allows extra properties. For JVM services that move money, pick Avro or Protobuf: small, fast and checked.

try.title: Ask a real registry
steps: From the labs folder, start the broker with Schema Registry: docker compose -f env/kafka.yml --profile schemas up -d --wait. The registry takes about a minute the first time.

sections.h: Kafka Connect moves data in and out, so you don't write that loop
sections.html:
Sooner or later every team writes the same two programs. One reads rows from a database and publishes them. The other reads a topic and writes the records somewhere else: an S3 bucket for the data lake, an Elasticsearch index for the support team. Both need what lessons 5 to 8 built by hand: batching, retries, a bookmark that survives a crash, several copies running at once, and a way to turn records into bytes and back.

Kafka Connect is that program, written once. It's a runtime that ships with Kafka, and you configure it instead of coding it. Its parts:

  • A worker is a JVM process that runs Connect. In distributed mode, workers with the same group.id form a Connect cluster and share the work through Kafka's group protocol, the way consumers share partitions (lesson 7). When a worker dies, the others take over its work.
  • A connector is one configured copy job: a plugin class plus settings, created with a POST to the REST API on port 8083. A source connector reads an outside system and writes to Kafka; a sink connector reads Kafka and writes out.
  • A task does the copying. A connector splits its job into up to tasks.max tasks, and the cluster spreads them over its workers.
  • A converter turns Connect's internal records into the bytes in Kafka and back: JsonConverter, StringConverter, or a registry-aware Avro converter that registers schemas for you.
  • A transform (a single message transform, SMT) changes each record on the way: renames a field, masks a card number, sends the record to another topic.

Connect keeps its own state in three compacted Kafka topics: connect-configs for connector configurations, connect-status for which task runs where, and connect-offsets for each source connector's bookmark in its source. For a file source the bookmark is a line number; for a database it's a position in the database's own log. Kafka 4.4 (KIP-1209) adds connect-internal-topics.sh, so you can create those topics yourself with the settings you choose, and internal.topics.automatic.creation.enable to stop workers from creating them.

Connect only moves records. Which records a database source produces is up to the plugin, and the plugin that matters for payments reads the database's log. That's Debezium, in the next section.

sections.h: Change data capture and the outbox: one write, two systems
sections.html:
The payment service authorizes a payment, inserts a row into PostgreSQL and sends PaymentAuthorized to Kafka. Those are two writes to two systems, and nothing makes them atomic. If the service dies between them, the database holds a payment the ledger never hears about. Send first and commit second, and a crash leaves an event for a payment that doesn't exist. A retry doesn't help, because after a crash the service doesn't know which half happened. Lesson 9 showed that a Kafka transaction can't include the database: it covers Kafka writes and offsets only, and KIP-939's two-phase commit hasn't shipped.

The transactional outbox makes it one write. The service inserts the payment row and an event row into an outbox table in the same database transaction, so both commit or neither does. Then something else moves outbox rows to Kafka.

The simplest mover polls: SELECT * FROM outbox WHERE sent = false every second, publish, mark as sent. That's a query per second on the payments database, up to a second of delay, and an ordering trap: rows become visible in commit order, not id order, so a poller that pages by id skips a row whose transaction committed late.

A better mover reads the database's own log. PostgreSQL writes every change to its write-ahead log (WAL) before it changes a table (lesson 1 compared Kafka's log to it). With wal_level=logical, it can decode the WAL into row changes for a client: that's change data capture (CDC). A replication slot is the client's bookmark. PostgreSQL keeps all WAL after the slot's confirmed position until the client confirms more. The Try-it reads a slot by hand: a committed transaction comes out as BEGIN, two inserts and COMMIT; a rolled-back one never comes out.

Debezium 3.7 is a Kafka Connect source connector that does this for you. It reads its slot with the pgoutput plugin, turns each row change into a change event, and stores its position, the LSN (log sequence number), in connect-offsets. Its outbox event router turns each outbox insert into a record on outbox.event.<aggregatetype>, keyed by aggregateid, with the payload as the value and the event id in a header named id. With the account as aggregateid, each account's events keep their order.

Delivery is at-least-once. Connect flushes the LSN about once a minute, and after a crash in between, Debezium sends the events since the last flush again, with the same ids. So consumers dedupe on the event id, as in lesson 6. And watch the slot: a slot that nobody reads keeps WAL forever, until the database's disk is full.

Through Debezium, the committed outbox row became one record keyed by the account, with the event id and type in headers, and the rolled-back payment produced nothing. analogy: A schema is the printed form a payment slip uses: named boxes in a fixed order. The registry is the office that approves new versions of the form, and its rule (BACKWARD) is that a clerk holding the new form must still be able to read every old slip in the archive; a new box is fine if the form says what to assume when it's empty. The outbox is a carbon set: the branch writes the payment and the courier's note on the same sheet, so one can't exist without the other. CDC is the courier reading the carbon copies in the order they were stamped and remembering the last stamp number. The analogy breaks at the courier: after losing its place, Debezium may deliver a note twice, so head office must recognise a note by its number.
world: Your services write to Oracle, and the same pattern works there: Debezium's Oracle connector reads the redo log through LogMiner, and the outbox event router doesn't care which database fed it. A Quarkus service can write the outbox row in the same JTA transaction as the payment (Debezium also ships a Quarkus outbox extension that does this from a CDI event). A Temporal activity that writes a payment and must announce it should write the outbox row in its own database transaction, not call a Kafka producer. On the schema side, register schemas from CI and set the producers' serializer to auto.register.schemas=false, so a deploy can't slip a new version past review; and choose BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE for compacted topics such as account state, where version 1 records never go away.
mistake: Unblocking a deploy by setting the subject's compatibility to NONE. The registry refused the new schema for a reason: some consumer, or some old record in the topic, can't be read with it. With NONE the version goes in, the producer deploys, and the failure moves to a consumer at 3 a.m., or to the replay next month. The fix is to make the change compatible: give the new field a default, or rename in two steps (add the new field with a default, move readers over, remove the old field later). Run the compatibility check in CI against the real registry, and keep auto.register.schemas=false in production producers so that only reviewed versions get registered.

kotlin.title: Kotlin

Java closes the statements with try-with-resources; Kotlin uses use, and its raw string builds the JSON payload without escapes. Neither touches Kafka: the service's only write is to its database, and Debezium publishes the event once the commit is in the WAL. If executeUpdate throws, the connection closes without a commit, PostgreSQL rolls back, and neither row exists.

steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. All 15 fail. They need no Docker: the schema tests compare your rule with Avro's own SchemaCompatibility, and the outbox tests replay what Debezium did in the Try-it.

In CompatibilityChecker.kt, write readProblems(reader, writer): names must match; then for every reader field, a type the writer's type can't be promoted to is a TYPE_MISMATCH, and a field the writer lacks with no default is a READER_FIELD_MISSING_DEFAULT_VALUE. canPromote is given.

In relay, a LinkedHashMap<Long, List<ChangeEvent>> from transaction id to its changes is enough; the commit entry says when to emit them.

drill.title: The reader rule from memory
drill.prompt: Write, from memory, the rule that decides whether a reader schema can read data written with a writer schema, as a function over field lists (names, types, defaults). Then answer: under FORWARD, can you remove currency from the schema if version 2 gave it a default? And under BACKWARD, can you add merchantId without one?

answer.html: fun readProblems(reader: RecordSchema, writer: RecordSchema): List<String> { if (reader.name != writer.name) return listOf("NAME_MISMATCH") val written = writer.fields.associateBy { it.name } return reader.fields.mapNotNull { f -> val w = written[f.name] when { w != null && !canPromote(w.type, f.type) -> "TYPE_MISMATCH: ${f.name}" w == null && !f.hasDefault -> "READER_FIELD_MISSING_DEFAULT_VALUE: ${f.name}" else -> null // same field, or the reader's default fills it; extra writer fields are skipped } } } // FORWARD, remove currency: yes. Old readers (v2) have currency with a default, so they read new records. // BACKWARD, add merchantId with no default: no. A new reader can't fill it from old records: HTTP 409.

alt.html: // record Field(String name, FieldType type, boolean hasDefault) {} // record RecordSchema(String name, List<Field> fields) {} static List<String> readProblems(RecordSchema reader, RecordSchema writer) { if (!reader.name().equals(writer.name())) return List.of("NAME_MISMATCH"); Map<String, Field> written = new HashMap<>(); for (Field f : writer.fields()) written.put(f.name(), f); List<String> problems = new ArrayList<>(); for (Field f : reader.fields()) { Field w = written.get(f.name()); if (w != null && !canPromote(w.type(), f.type())) problems.add("TYPE_MISMATCH: " + f.name()); else if (w == null && !f.hasDefault()) problems.add("READER_FIELD_MISSING_DEFAULT_VALUE: " + f.name()); // otherwise: same field, or the reader's default fills it; extra writer fields are skipped } return problems; } // FORWARD, remove currency: yes. Old readers (v2) have currency with a default, so they read new records. // BACKWARD, add merchantId with no default: no. A new reader can't fill it from old records: HTTP 409.

recap: Brokers store bytes. A schema says what the bytes mean, and the registry gives each schema an id that the serializer puts in front of every record: a 0 byte and 4 bytes of id.
Avro reads with two schemas, the writer's and the reader's, matched by field name: extra writer fields are skipped, missing ones take the reader's default, and a missing field with no default fails.
BACKWARD (the default) means new readers read old data: upgrade consumers first. FORWARD means old readers read new data: producers first. FULL needs both; _TRANSITIVE checks every version.
Kafka Connect runs copy jobs: workers form a cluster, connectors split into tasks, converters turn records into bytes, transforms edit them, and source offsets live in connect-offsets.
The transactional outbox writes the business row and the event row in one database transaction. CDC reads them from the write-ahead log, committed transactions only, in commit order.
Debezium stores its WAL position (LSN) as its offset and is at-least-once: after a crash it repeats events with the same id, so consumers dedupe on it.

explain.prompt: A colleague's payment service inserts the payment into PostgreSQL and then calls producer.send. Explain what can go wrong, why a retry or a Kafka transaction doesn't fix it, and how the outbox with Debezium does.
explain.answer: They are two writes to two systems with nothing tying them together. A crash after the insert and before the send leaves a payment that no consumer hears about; sending first leaves an event for a payment that may never commit. After a crash the service doesn't know which half happened, so a retry can't put it right. A Kafka transaction only covers Kafka writes and offsets, and the two-phase commit proposal, KIP-939, isn't released. With the outbox, the service writes the payment row and an event row in one PostgreSQL transaction, so both exist or neither does. Debezium reads the committed rows from the write-ahead log through a replication slot, in commit order, and the outbox event router publishes each event with the account as key. Rolled-back transactions never reach the log reader. Debezium can repeat events after a crash, because it stores its WAL position only about once a minute, so the consumers dedupe on the event id in the same transaction as their own effect.

deeper.html:
Optional fields in Avro. A field that may be missing is a union with null and a null default: {"name": "note", "type": ["null", "string"], "default": null}. The default must match the first type in the union, which is why null comes first.

Subject names. The default TopicNameStrategy gives one schema per topic (payments-value). RecordNameStrategy and TopicRecordNameStrategy name the subject after the record type, so one topic can carry several event types, each with its own evolution, for example PaymentAuthorized and PaymentCaptured on one partition to keep their order.

The initial snapshot. When a Debezium connector starts with no stored offset, snapshot.mode=initial reads the tables it captures first and emits each existing row as a read event (op = r). That's why the Try-it's topic started with the row from the WAL peek. For an outbox you usually want only new rows: set snapshot.mode=no_data.

Slot lag. SELECT slot_name, active, confirmed_flush_lsn, pg_current_wal_lsn() FROM pg_replication_slots; shows how far each slot is behind. A connector that is stopped for a weekend keeps its slot, and PostgreSQL keeps every byte of WAL since then. Alert on it, and drop slots you no longer need.

Oracle. Debezium's Oracle connector reads redo logs through LogMiner by default. The model is the same, a log of committed changes read with a stored position (an SCN instead of an LSN), with more setup: supplemental logging and a LogMiner user.
